title: After the plague
text: When the Black Death reached England in 1348, it killed perhaps half the population within two years. Yet the survivors' descendants inherited a world that was, in some ways, {{1}}. Labour had become scarce, and scarce labour {{2}} a price: wages roughly doubled within a generation, and serfs found that landlords now had to {{3}} for their services rather than simply command them. Parliament tried to {{4}} the change with a statute fixing wages at pre-plague levels, and when that failed, officials took to tracking down workers who refused to return to their lords. Economic gravity proved stronger than the law. Rents fell, cultivation moved from marginal land to better soil, and historians {{5}} that the plague, by thinning the workforce, {{6}} the end of feudalism by a century or more. The authorities' response to the upheaval also left a {{7}} in the law books: sumptuary laws that tried to stop labourers dressing above their station are an early chapter in the long history of turning economic anxiety into {{8}} about clothes, manners and morals.

gaps.explanation: 'a world that was, in some ways, freer' — offering more liberty; the context of rising wages rules out frailer, fresher and frostier.
'scarce labour commanded a price' — fetched one, as goods 'command a high price'; quote and charge would make the workers the sellers, and value does not take this object.
'landlords had to bid for their services' — compete with offers; bet takes 'on', bow takes 'to'.
'tried to reverse the change' — undo it; revise = alter a plan, revert = go back (intransitive).
'historians claim that…' — assert with an argument; acclaim = praise, proclaim = announce publicly and formally.
'accelerated the end of feudalism by a century' — speeded it up; accompany would only mean occur alongside, and 'by a century' demands a change of timing.
'left a trace in the law books' — a remaining sign; tract = an area of land or a pamphlet, trance = a dreamlike state.
'turning anxiety into rules about clothes' — regulations; rumour = unverified talk, raid = a sudden attack.
